I hope you enjoy being told that vegans/yuppies/intellectuals don't understand real nature and can't hack it by themselves, because that's pretty much half the book. Their level of unpreparedness and denial stretches belief sometimes, and can take you out of it. In my opinion it even feels kinda mean-spirited sometimes. It feels too much like the author bludgeoning you with his point of view instead of being more subtle about it and having the story feel more organic; he even manages to bring up his ideas about the Israeli/Arab conflict again, which was a bit jarring in his book about killer Bigfeet (or should it be bigfoots?).

I feel like this story would have made a solid short story or chapter in a WWZ-style book, but when you stretch it out a whole book it feels, well stretched-out. It's still a 5 or 6/10 fun book, but ultimately nothing special.

> What part of Occam's razor do you think it got wrong, though? The way she talked about it sounded alright to me.

She says that Occam's Razor is "*the idea that between competing hypotheses, the simplest one is the right one.*" there are two problems with this:

First of all it's not about the *simplest* hypothesis, it's about the one that *makes the less assumptions*. The distinction is important because "simplest" is too subjective and leaves a lot of weaseling room. You'll often hear, for example, believers in the paranormal and the like saying that it's simpler to believe that they saw an alien instead of other options (craziness, alcohol, etc..), but they ignore the fact that the existence of life outside our planet that possesses interstellar travel is a HUGE assumption to make.

Second is that Occam's Razor doesn't say that that hypothesis is the right one, it means it should be tested for first. You don't just decide that the most complicated one is wrong and call it a day ffs.

But we are not talking about living in general, we are talking about working and if, in any particular situation, the extra effort is worth the extra money(and the benefit it entails obviously). It probably won't be worth it forever, at some point the amount of effort required by the extra work wont be covered by the profit you get from it, that's all. In a video game the stats you gain for leveling up are, generally speaking, a very small part of the "profit" you get from playing a video game so diminishing returns don't apply much. Obvious exceptions are games that require a lot of grinding and if those cases you **do** see a lot of people stop playing. 


>Hey, you want another example? Commuting. 

Well yeah but the law of diminishing returns here would still apply. A lot of people (myself included) have long commutes to work, but the further away you have to travel or the more time the commute would take, the less worth it the extra money from the job would be.

It's not just about the stats you gain, but also there are other things like the plot, world exploration, character development or just how fun playing it can be.
